evaluated.name: Depreciation Neutral Cash Backing Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(oancf, dp), ib), at), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Earnings yield is rewarded only where reported income is persistently matched by depreciation-neutral cash earnings; when income runs ahead of cash earnings net of D&A, the low price reflects accrual-inflated, non-repeatable profits rather than mispricing.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the naive oancf > ib test with (oancf - dp) - ib removes the mechanical D&A addback that made the old gate switched on for nearly every firm, so the quality channel now splits the cross-section roughly evenly and genuinely discriminates. The gate is also made continuous and three-year smoothed, eliminating the degenerate zero mass point that previously sat in the middle of the sort, and the multiplicative rank form means cheapness only scores highly where cash backing is durable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Weakest Link Value Solvency
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), MIN(RANK(RATIO(re, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap stock is only a quality value stock if it also has accumulated retained earnings and enough operating cash flow to service its liabilities; a firm failing on any one leg is a distress candidate, so the score should be set by its weakest dimension rather than by an average.
evaluated.reasoning: The MIN operator is a conjunctive, weight-free aggregator that answers the arbitrary 50/25/25 weighting complaint directly: no strong leg can compensate for a weak one, which is exactly the value-trap logic that an additive composite dilutes. The quality legs are deliberately balance-sheet and debt-service based (retained earnings intensity, cash flow to total liabilities) rather than gross profitability and earnings stability, so this is not a repackaging of the published QMJ/Novy-Marx quality-value stack, and all inputs are contemporaneous so coverage stays high.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Conservative Earnings Yield
evaluated.expression: RATIO(MIN(ib, SUB(oancf, dp)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
evaluated.hypothesis: The market should be valued on the lower of reported income and depreciation-charged cash earnings; firms whose price is low relative to this conservative earnings base are cheap on the earnings number that is hardest to manage, whereas firms cheap only on reported income are accrual-inflated.
evaluated.reasoning: Subtracting dp before comparing to income neutralizes the D&A addback that made a naive oancf-versus-ib gate switch on almost everywhere, so the MIN genuinely binds for roughly half the cross-section and embeds the quality test inside the valuation multiple rather than beside it. Unlike the failed weakest-link rank screen, the MIN here operates on economic quantities in dollars, not on ranks, so it does not select stale low-growth firms and it produces a continuous, well-behaved yield variable that should sharpen the Fama-MacBeth slope.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap With Widening Gross Margin
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 5), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, a multi-year widening of the gross margin signals restored pricing power and mean-reverting mispricing, while a narrowing margin signals competitive erosion that justifies the low multiple.
evaluated.reasoning: The conditioner is a dynamic state (five-year slope of unit economics) rather than a level, which distinguishes recovering value from melting value in a way no static profitability or accrual measure can. Margin trend is measured before overhead and financing, so it is less contaminated by the earnings management that drives the accrual channels, making this an economically independent test.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Depreciation Conservatism Conditioned Earnings Yield
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, those charging depreciation at or above their own recent norm are reporting conservatively understated earnings and are genuinely cheap, while those whose depreciation intensity has fallen below their historical rate are propping up reported income through useful-life and write-off policy, so their low multiple is manufactured.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the gross-profitability conditioner that merely rediscovers Novy-Marx and QMJ and instead conditions value on an accounting-policy channel — the firm's own depreciation intensity relative to its three-year norm — which is a discretion-based quality measure rather than a profitability level. Benchmarking against the firm's own history rather than the cross-section removes capital-intensity differences, so the conditioner isolates policy change, and the signed z-score puts cheap-with-shrinking-depreciation firms in the short leg where the earnings-inflation trap lives.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Non Cash Working Capital Bloat Versus Sales
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale), 1), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high EBITDA yield is a bargain only when each dollar of sales still requires the same or less non-cash working capital; when receivables and inventories net of operating payables rise per dollar of sales, the cheap firm is channel-stuffing or accumulating unsold goods and the discount is warranted.
evaluated.reasoning: The accrual measure is rebuilt as (act - che) - (lct - dlc), explicitly stripping cash and short-term debt so that cash accumulation or debt paydown is no longer misread as accrual bloat, fixing the internal inconsistency the critic identified. Expressing it as a change in working capital intensity of sales rather than a change scaled by assets makes it an operating-efficiency deterioration measure benchmarked to the firm's own revenue base, which is a sharper trap detector than the level accrual sort.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Earned Versus Contributed Book Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(re, ceq), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Book-to-market only identifies mispricing when the book value was earned rather than raised: a cheap firm whose equity is mostly accumulated retained earnings has demonstrated cash-generating capacity, while a cheap firm whose equity is mostly contributed capital has funded past losses with issuance and its book value carries no evidence of profitability.
evaluated.reasoning: The conditioner is the composition of book equity, not a leverage or solvency ratio, so it avoids the mechanical channel where debt inflates book-to-market and the sort degenerates into a leverage sort — the flaw in both the net-cash version and the earlier weakest-link screen. It also differs from the failed re/at screen because the scaling is by book equity, making it a capital-origin mix that is independent of asset size and of the value leg's own denominator.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Payer Only Dividend Sustainability Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(INDICATOR(dvc, 0), RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(oancf, dp), dvc), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Within dividend payers, a high yield is mispricing when operating cash flow net of the depreciation charge comfortably exceeds the dividend, and is a pre-cut trap when the payout consumes essentially all maintenance-adjusted cash generation.
evaluated.reasoning: The payer indicator forces non-payers to exactly zero, and since the conditioner is a signed z-score centered near zero the payers straddle them, so both portfolio legs are populated by dividend payers rather than by non-payers sorted on a solvency ratio. The coverage measure is now the payout tested against maintenance-adjusted cash earnings (oancf minus dp minus dvc) rather than against total liabilities, matching the sustainability mechanism in the hypothesis while using a safe assets denominator that avoids dividing by a zero dividend.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Depreciation Deviation With EBITDA Yield Leg
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The depreciation-conservatism conditioner should work with any pre-depreciation valuation multiple; pairing it with EBITDA yield tests whether the effect comes from the accounting-discretion channel rather than from the bottom-line earnings yield itself.
evaluated.reasoning: EBITDA yield is mechanically independent of the depreciation charge, so if the winning gen-1 signal were merely picking up the arithmetic link between dp and ib, this variant would fail, whereas if the discretion story is right it should be at least as strong and cleaner. This is a deliberate leg-isolation experiment that also avoids the negative-earnings tail that distorts E/P sorts.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Depreciation Lagging Asset Growth
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(GROWTH(dp, 1), GROWTH(at, 1)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, a depreciation charge growing more slowly than the asset base signals stretched useful lives and capitalized costs that flatter reported income, so the low multiple is on inflated earnings; depreciation growing with or ahead of assets marks conservative recognition and genuine cheapness.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the own-history level deviation of the gen-1 winner with a flow-versus-flow comparison, which detects under-depreciation of newly acquired assets that a level ratio can miss when the asset base is expanding. It keeps the discretion mechanism that worked while testing a different and more direct measurement of it, and uses only one-year changes so coverage stays close to the winner's 0.14.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Persistent Cash Earnings Within Cheap Book
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(SUB(oancf, dp), dvc), 0), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Book-to-market identifies mispricing among firms that have repeatedly generated cash earnings in excess of maintenance and payout needs, while cheap firms that have only intermittently self-funded are traps whose discount reflects a genuine funding gap.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests persistence — a count of self-funding years — rather than the level of accumulated equity that inverted in gen 1, distinguishing a repeated-outcome quality concept from a stock-of-safety concept. If persistence also inverts, we will have learned that any cheap-and-safe conditioner is spanned by FF5 and can retire the whole family; if it works, it opens a frequency-based dimension the archive has not used.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Gross Profit To Cash Conversion Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), SUB(sale, cogs)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What separates quality value from a value trap is how much of the gross profit actually survives overhead, working capital and maintenance capital to become distributable cash; a cheap firm converting a high fraction of gross profit into maintenance-adjusted cash flow is mispriced, one converting little is running an uneconomic cost structure.
evaluated.reasoning: Conversion efficiency is a ratio of two quality quantities rather than a scaled level, so it is orthogonal to the gross-profitability level that Novy-Marx documented and to the accrual measures already in the archive. Pairing it with EBITDA yield keeps the valuation leg independent of the depreciation and cash-flow terms in the conditioner, so the interaction is not mechanically induced.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Earnings Smoothing Versus Cash Volatility
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(VOL(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), at), 5), VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 5)), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, those whose reported earnings are far smoother than their underlying maintenance-adjusted cash flows are using accrual discretion to mask a volatile business, so their low multiple rests on managed numbers; cheap firms whose earnings volatility matches their cash volatility are reporting honestly and are the genuine bargains.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the operating-liability construct entirely, avoiding both the sign conflict with the accrual/NOA evidence and the overlap with the already-tested working-capital signal, and instead measures the gap between cash-flow variability and earnings variability — a second-moment discretion measure with no first-moment accrual content. It stays inside the accounting-discretion family that has produced the archive's only reliable alphas (depreciation deviation, cash backing) while testing smoothing rather than recognition timing, and the NEG makes the short leg cheap-and-heavily-smoothed firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Verifiable Asset Backing Of Cheap Book
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(act, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Book-to-market is only informative when the book value is composed of assets whose carrying value is verifiable; cheap firms whose assets are predominantly current are unlikely to face impairments, whereas cheap firms whose book is concentrated in long-lived, hard-to-value assets carry stale book values that will be written down, which is exactly what makes them value traps.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the retained-earnings flow, which the critic correctly identified as payout-adjusted ROA and therefore spanned by RMW, and replaces it with a measurement-reliability conditioner on the numerator of the value ratio itself — an asset-composition concept with no profitability content. Industry z-scoring is essential here because asset mix is largely a sector characteristic, so the conditioner captures within-industry deviation in the verifiability of book value rather than a sector bet, and it introduces a write-down-risk channel the archive has never tested.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dual Measurement Reliability Value
evaluated.expression: RANK(MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ADD(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(act, at), 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap firms are mispriced when the numbers behind the cheapness are measurable — depreciation charged at or above the firm's own historical intensity and a balance sheet weighted toward verifiable current assets — and are traps when both the depreciation charge and the asset base are soft, since impairment and earnings restatement risk is concentrated there.
evaluated.reasoning: The two conditioners that produced the archive's only reliable alphas measure the same economic concept (reliability of long-lived asset accounting) through independent data — an income-statement policy deviation and a balance-sheet composition — so summing their comparably scaled z-scores should raise reliability without narrowing coverage. The outer RANK is a monotone transform that leaves the decile sort and therefore ls_alpha unchanged while replacing the skewed product with a uniform regressor, which directly targets the weak Fama-MacBeth slopes seen throughout this family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sales Yield With Depreciation Discipline
evaluated.expression: RANK(MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high sales-to-price ratio identifies firms the market has written off at the revenue level, and the mispricing is real when the firm is still charging full depreciation against those revenues; when depreciation has been quietly reduced, the apparent revenue cheapness coexists with hollowed-out asset recognition and no recovery follows.
evaluated.reasoning: Every valuation leg tested so far has been an earnings or EBITDA multiple, both of which are closely spanned by HML and RMW, whereas sales yield is a distinct valuation channel that survives loss-making firms and does not require positive earnings, widening the usable cross-section. Holding the winning depreciation conditioner fixed makes this a clean test of whether the interaction generalizes across the valuation dimension or is specific to profit-based multiples.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unit Cost Stability Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(VOL(RATIO(cogs, sale), 5), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap firms with stable cost of goods per dollar of sales operate a controllable production process whose depressed multiple is more likely to be sentiment-driven, whereas cheap firms whose unit costs swing widely face input-price or scale instability that makes future earnings genuinely unforecastable and the discount warranted.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's only volatility test compared earnings versus cash-flow variability, an accrual-smoothing concept that failed; unit-cost variability is instead a real operating-process attribute measured entirely above the accrual line, so it tests the stability channel where it has economic content rather than accounting content. It also complements the depreciation and asset-composition channels by describing the income statement's input side, keeping the batch's mechanisms non-overlapping.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Operating Versus Cash Asset Backing Contrast
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SUB(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, che), at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(che, at), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Book value backed by operating current assets — receivables and inventory that are periodically realized in cash and therefore continuously validated — protects a cheap firm from being a trap, whereas book value backed by an idle cash pile conveys liquidity but no evidence that the operating book is worth carrying value.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than substituting one term into the gen-2 winner, this makes the conditioner an explicit contrast between the two components of act/at, so the outcome identifies the driver: a positive alpha attributes the 5.5 t-stat to operating-asset verifiability while a negative alpha attributes it to cash holdings, and near-zero says the two channels are offsetting. Both components are industry z-scored before differencing so the contrast is measured among firms with comparable working-capital norms rather than across sectors.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Depreciation Per Revenue Versus Own Norm
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, sale), MA(RATIO(dp, sale), 5)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically meaningful recognition test is whether the firm still charges the same depreciation per dollar of revenue it historically charged; cheap firms whose depreciation per revenue has slipped below their own five-year norm are deferring the cost of capital consumption, so their earnings and hence their apparent cheapness are overstated.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the year-over-year growth difference with a level deviation removes the noisy dp growth term and, because neither side of the difference is a growth rate, it cannot be a repackaged asset-growth or sales-growth anomaly — the critic's core objection to the previous flow versions. Scaling by revenue rather than assets also ties the charge to the operating base actually being consumed, which is the quantity the recognition hypothesis is about, and the five-year norm makes the benchmark stable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Enterprise Cheapness With Verifiable Assets
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(act, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness measured against the whole capital structure rather than equity alone identifies firms whose operating assets are priced low irrespective of financing, and such cheapness is mispricing when the asset base is verifiable and a justified discount when the book is dominated by opaque long-lived assets facing impairment.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the five-point TS_RANK value leg, which the critic rightly identified as a coarse, price-path-driven long-horizon reversal proxy, and replaces it with a continuous enterprise-value multiple — a valuation dimension the archive has never tested and one that removes the mechanical leverage inflation contaminating equity multiples. Holding the strongest conditioner fixed makes this a clean test of whether the measurement-reliability interaction survives when cheapness is defined at the asset rather than the equity level.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap With Near Term Obligation Cover
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm holding cash in excess of its current liabilities cannot be forced into distressed asset sales or dilutive financing, so its discount is more likely sentiment; a cheap firm whose near-term obligations exceed its cash must transact under pressure, and the discount reflects that funding constraint.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-3 contrast test showed the strong act/at alpha came from the cash component, since subtracting cash from current assets flipped the alpha to -4.1%, so the correct refinement is to measure cash against the obligations it must actually cover rather than against total assets. Netting current liabilities keeps this distinct from the failed total-leverage and weakest-link solvency screens, which measured long-run capital structure rather than the immediate funding gap that turns a cheap firm into a forced seller.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Standardized Depreciation Cut
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), VOL(RATIO(dp, at), 5)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What signals accounting discretion is not the size of a change in depreciation intensity but its size relative to how much that firm's depreciation intensity normally moves; a one-point drop is meaningful for a firm with a stable charge and meaningless for a firm with a lumpy asset base.
evaluated.reasoning: The raw deviation is dominated cross-sectionally by capital-intensity heterogeneity, so standardizing by the firm's own five-year volatility of dp/at converts it into a firm-specific surprise measure that should be far cleaner in the middle of the distribution — precisely where the current family's Fama-MacBeth slope is weak. This is a measurement refinement to the archive's best-performing mechanism rather than a new channel, appropriate now that the mechanism is established.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Downside Only Depreciation Discretion
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), ABS(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The information in depreciation policy is one-sided: cutting the charge below the firm's own norm inflates earnings and marks a trap, whereas charging more than the norm is ordinary asset renewal or conservatism that carries no additional good news.
evaluated.reasoning: The construction SUB(x, ABS(x)) is exactly twice the negative part of the deviation, so all firms at or above their norm are pooled and only the cutters are ordered, which tests whether the family's alpha comes from shorting earnings-inflating traps or from a symmetric spread. Knowing which side carries the payoff determines whether future refinements should target trap identification or bargain identification, and an asymmetric signal that concentrates the short leg may raise both alpha and its t-stat.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Overhead Burden Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), ebitda), sale), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, a heavy overhead burden — the gap between gross profit and EBITDA per dollar of sales — means fixed costs will consume any revenue recovery, so the discount is deserved; lean-overhead cheap firms convert a revenue rebound straight into profit and are the genuine bargains.
evaluated.reasoning: The difference between gross profit and EBITDA isolates selling and administrative cost intensity, an income-statement dimension the archive has never touched — prior tests covered gross margin level, margin trend and unit-cost volatility but never the overhead layer that sits between them. Industry z-scoring is necessary because overhead intensity is largely a business-model characteristic, so the conditioner measures within-industry cost bloat rather than a sector bet.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Normalized Depreciation Earnings Yield
evaluated.expression: RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(at, MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3))), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
evaluated.hypothesis: Restating earnings with the depreciation charge the firm would have taken at its own three-year average intensity strips out the discretionary component of the charge, so the resulting yield ranks firms by cheapness on capital-consumption-honest earnings rather than on reported earnings.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the additive rank stack — which the critic correctly noted would have its slope dominated by the earnings-yield leg and could not distinguish separability from value rediscovery — with a single continuous multiple in which the quality adjustment lives inside the numerator, so a firm cheap only because it under-depreciated is mechanically demoted rather than merely down-weighted. Because the output is a smooth yield rather than a skewed rank product, it is the natural candidate to fix the family's weak Fama-MacBeth slope while preserving the depreciation-discretion mechanism that generates the alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Discretion Spread Inside The Cheap Tail
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The depreciation-discretion effect is not a smooth cross-sectional slope but a segmentation effect operating only among already-cheap firms, where accounting honesty decides whether a low multiple reflects mispricing or an impending earnings reset; among expensive firms the same accounting information carries no return implication.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a diagnosis of the archive's persistent alpha-versus-fmb divergence rather than another composite: it hard-gates the conditioner to the cheapest 30% of firms and leaves everyone else at exactly zero in the neutral middle, so both portfolio legs are drawn from the value segment and the resulting spread is a pure quality-value versus value-trap comparison. If alpha holds or improves while the pooled Fama-MacBeth slope stays weak, we learn definitively that the effect is segment-specific and that pooled cross-sectional slopes are the wrong statistic for this mechanism; if alpha collapses, the effect needs the expensive side and the multiplicative form is doing real work.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Depreciation Rate On Long Lived Assets
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, SUB(at, act)), MA(RATIO(dp, SUB(at, act)), 3)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Depreciation is charged against long-lived assets only, so the economically correct discretion measure is the charge per dollar of non-current assets; scaling by total assets mixes in working-capital-heavy firms whose low dp/at reflects business model rather than policy.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a measurement correction to the archive's best mechanism, not a new channel: the deviation is computed on the actual depreciable base, which should sharpen the conditioner most for firms whose current-asset share is changing and reduce the cross-sectional noise that has kept the family's Fama-MacBeth slopes near 1.7. It also inherits the gen-2 finding that the interaction is not mechanical, since the EBITDA-yield leg contains no depreciation term.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Bounded Discretion And Liquidity Conditioner
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm is mispriced rather than trapped when it both charges honest depreciation and holds cash sufficient to cover its near-term obligations, and the two requirements should be combined as ordinal conditions rather than as raw magnitudes because each is informative through its rank, not its scale.
evaluated.reasoning: Previous composites summed two winsorized z-scores, letting whichever channel had fatter tails dominate and dragging Sharpe from 0.51 to 0.26; SUMRANK bounds each channel before combining, so the conditioner is a genuine two-condition score rather than a tail-weighted average. The two inputs are the archive's only conditioners with independently positive alpha and they use unrelated data — income-statement policy and balance-sheet liquidity — so a bounded combination is the best remaining candidate for raising reliability without sacrificing the Sharpe of the depreciation leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Peer Benchmarked Depreciation Rate
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(dp, SUB(at, act)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Useful-life assumptions are comparable within an industry, so a cheap firm depreciating its long-lived assets more slowly than its industry peers is using discretion to flatter earnings even if its own history shows no change — a firm that has always been aggressive never registers on a self-benchmarked measure.
evaluated.reasoning: Every depreciation test so far benchmarks the firm against itself, which by construction misses persistently aggressive reporters, and the peer benchmark is the one alternative that captures the level rather than the change in conservatism. Industry z-scoring is essential because asset lives differ enormously across sectors, and pairing it with the same EBITDA-yield leg makes the self-versus-peer benchmark the only design difference being tested.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Chronic Depreciation Conservatism Count
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 0), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What distinguishes an honest reporter from an opportunistic one is not the size of a single year's deviation but how habitually the firm charges above its own norm; a cheap firm that has been consistently conservative for several consecutive years has no hidden earnings inflation left to unwind, while a firm that is conservative only occasionally is managing the charge episodically.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a frequency conditioner, not a linear part of the deviation, so it is not implied by decomposing the symmetric and downside results — two firms with identical current deviations receive different scores depending on their record, which is exactly the information a magnitude measure discards. A three-year count keeps the history requirement modest so coverage stays near the family's 0.13, and the discreteness of the count spreads firms across a handful of well-populated groups rather than into thin tails, which is where the family's cross-sectional slope has been leaking.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Impairment Exposure Weighted Discretion
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, SUB(at, act)), MA(RATIO(dp, SUB(at, act)), 3)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(at, act), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Depreciation discretion only matters economically in proportion to how much of the balance sheet is exposed to it: for an asset-heavy cheap firm a shortfall in the charge translates into a large overstatement of both earnings and book value, while for an asset-light firm the same policy deviation is economically trivial.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a rescaling of the conditioner but an exposure weighting: the non-negative long-lived-asset share amplifies the signed discretion score, so cheap asset-heavy under-depreciators are pushed to the short extreme and cheap asset-heavy conservatives to the long extreme, while asset-light firms are compressed toward neutral regardless of their policy. It converts the conditioner from a uniform-treatment-effect assumption into one where treatment intensity varies with the firm's actual depreciable base, which is the economically correct specification and should sharpen both tails.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Impairment Adjusted Book To Market
evaluated.expression: RATIO(SUB(ceq, TS_SUM(SUB(MUL(at, MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), dp), 3)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
evaluated.hypothesis: Book equity is overstated by the cumulative amount of depreciation a firm failed to charge relative to its own normal intensity, so writing that shortfall off the book gives a cheapness measure on assets that will survive audit; firms that look cheap only before the adjustment are carrying stale asset values.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than averaging two highly correlated price multiples, this changes the quantity being priced: the quality adjustment is applied cumulatively to the balance sheet rather than to one year's earnings, which moves firms materially across book-to-market deciles instead of merely reweighting them. The earnings-side embedding produced a strong cross-sectional slope but no alpha because it stayed close to E/P; a book-side embedding tests whether the same discretion information carries portfolio value when it is capitalized over three years into the value anchor itself.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Industry Neutral Cheapness With Discretion
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness is only informative relative to firms with comparable asset lives and capital intensity, so ranking EBITDA yield within industry isolates genuine mispricing rather than the permanent multiple differences between capital-intensive and asset-light sectors, and the depreciation-discretion conditioner then operates on a homogeneous set of candidates.
evaluated.reasoning: Every version of the winning family has used an unconditional cross-sectional value rank, which loads the long leg on structurally low-multiple industries whose returns FF5's HML already spans, so industry-neutralizing the value leg is the one untested design choice that can raise abnormal return and Sharpe simultaneously rather than trading one metric for the other. It also aligns the two legs, since the conditioner's economic meaning — depreciation policy relative to a norm — is inherently within-industry.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Magnitude Plus Chronicity Discretion
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ADD(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)), ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 0), 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm is most credibly mispriced when its depreciation charge is both currently far above its norm and has been above it repeatedly, because a single large deviation can be an asset-mix accident while a persistent pattern reveals a conservative reporting policy.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has cleanly separated the two statistical roles — magnitude carries the alpha (4.9%, t=4.76, Sharpe 0.51) and chronicity carries the cross-sectional slope (fmb 3.62) — and these are different functions of the same underlying deviation, so summing their standardized versions is a targeted attempt to obtain both forms of evidence rather than a generic composite. Because both legs derive from one economic channel they should reinforce rather than dilute, unlike the earlier composites that mixed accounting policy with balance-sheet liquidity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Slide From Peak Recognition
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, at), 5)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Under-recognition accumulates gradually, so the informative benchmark is the highest depreciation intensity the firm has ever sustained: a cheap firm still charging near its historical peak has nothing deferred, while one whose charge has drifted far below its own peak has been progressively capitalizing costs that a moving average partially absorbs into the benchmark.
evaluated.reasoning: A three-year moving average is contaminated by the very drift it is meant to detect — a firm that cuts depreciation each year pulls its own benchmark down and looks innocent — whereas a five-year maximum is a ratchet benchmark immune to that contamination. This is a different benchmark concept rather than a rescaling, and because the measure retains magnitude it should preserve the tail behaviour that generates alpha in this family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hidden Depreciation Shortfall Per Price
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(MUL(at, MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), dp), 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically relevant quantity is the accumulated dollar amount of depreciation a firm has failed to charge, measured against what investors are paying: a cheap firm carrying a large hidden shortfall relative to its market value faces an earnings reset that the low multiple has not discounted, while one with no accumulated shortfall is cheap on clean numbers.
evaluated.reasoning: Capitalizing the shortfall over three years and scaling by market capitalization converts the annual policy deviation into a stock of overstatement expressed in the same units as the valuation, which is the natural way to compare the size of the accounting problem to the size of the discount. It repairs the gen-5 failure in which the same cumulative quantity was subtracted from book equity and produced a strong slope but no alpha, by using it as a conditioner on cheapness rather than as the value anchor itself.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Long Lived Asset Utilization Within Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(sale, SUB(at, act)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm whose long-lived assets still turn over a normal volume of revenue owns productive capacity that the market is discounting, whereas a cheap firm generating little revenue per dollar of fixed assets is carrying idle or obsolete capacity whose book value will eventually be written down — the operating counterpart of the accounting-recognition trap.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the liquidity ablation entirely and opens an asset-utilization channel the archive has never tested, measuring whether the depreciable base is economically employed rather than how it is depreciated or how much cash sits beside it. Levels rather than growth rates keep it clear of the asset-growth confound, and industry z-scoring is required because revenue per fixed asset is an order of magnitude different across sectors, so the conditioner captures within-industry underutilization.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Recentered Conjunctive Quality Screen
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm qualifies as a bargain only if it clears both hurdles — depreciation charged at least in line with its own norm and cash covering near-term obligations — so its quality score should be the weaker of the two conditions, with firms failing either one classified as traps.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic's objection was purely a construction defect: MIN of two un-recentered z-scores has a strongly negative mean, so the product loaded negatively on cheapness for most firms, exactly the flaw behind the archived weakest-link inversion. Wrapping the MIN in an outer ZSCORE restores a zero mean so that roughly half the cross-section receives positive weight on cheapness and half negative, which preserves the intended long leg of cheap-and-doubly-clean firms and short leg of cheap-and-failing firms while keeping the conjunctive economics that distinguishes this test from the archived additive composite.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Conjunction With Leverage Not Liquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(lt, at), 1))))))
evaluated.hypothesis: If the conjunctive screen works because a cheap firm must clear both an accounting-honesty hurdle and a balance-sheet-survival hurdle, then substituting total-liability burden for cash cover should reproduce the effect; if it works only with cash, the second hurdle is specifically about immediate funding rather than solvency generally.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the decisive content-versus-structure test for the archive's best-performing design: the conjunctive operator and the depreciation leg are held fixed and only the survival condition changes from near-term cash cover to overall leverage. Because leverage-based conditioners have consistently inverted in additive form here, a positive result would demonstrate that the nonlinear weakest-link structure, not the choice of safety variable, is what rescues the interaction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Discrete Two Hurdle Quality Score
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 0), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 0))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters is not how far a cheap firm clears each hurdle but how many hurdles it clears at all: passing both the depreciation-honesty and cash-cover tests is the qualitative distinction between quality value and a value trap.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive shows magnitude carries alpha through fat tails while ordinal measures carry the slope, so a discrete zero-one-two score is the extreme ordinal case — it pools firms into three well-populated groups, which should produce a stable Fama-MacBeth slope and portfolio legs that do not rotate on outliers. It also implements the same two economic conditions as the conjunctive screen but with an additive-in-counts rather than weakest-link aggregation, isolating whether the nonlinearity or the discreteness is what helps.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Asset Scaled Hidden Shortfall
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(MUL(at, MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), dp), 3), at), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The accumulated three-year depreciation shortfall is an earnings-quality stock that should be measured against the asset base that generated it, and cheap firms carrying a large shortfall per dollar of assets face an unavoidable future earnings reset.
evaluated.reasoning: The market-cap-scaled version produced alpha of 3.2% with a completely flat slope (fmb 0.06), exactly the signature of a mechanical second 1/price term interacting with the value leg's own inverse-price, so rescaling by assets removes the size tilt and tests whether the cumulative-shortfall concept has standalone content. If the alpha survives with a positive slope, the cumulative stock is genuinely informative; if it vanishes, the earlier result was a price artifact and the family should stay with annual deviations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Deleveraging Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, the direction of the liability burden matters more than its level: a firm actively shrinking liabilities relative to assets has creditor support and internal cash generation, whereas one whose liability burden is rising is financing losses and its discount reflects an accelerating claim of debtholders on equity value.
evaluated.reasoning: Every balance-sheet conditioner tested so far has been a level — leverage, cash, current assets — and levels of safety have repeatedly inverted because they are spanned by the factor model, whereas the one-year change in liability intensity is a flow that captures where the firm is heading rather than where it stands. It is also the only remaining untested channel that speaks directly to the distress side of the value-trap story without duplicating the depreciation or liquidity legs.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Three Source Weakest Link Screen
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)), MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt), 1))))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm survives the trap classification only if it clears three hurdles drawn from three different statements — honest depreciation recognition on the income statement, cash covering near-term obligations on the balance sheet, and maintenance-adjusted operating cash flow covering total liabilities on the cash-flow statement — and failing the weakest of these is what defines a value trap.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that a chronicity count built from the same dp/at deviation is a correlated relabelling rather than an independent hurdle, so the third condition is replaced by debt-service capacity measured from cash flow, which shares no input with either existing leg. Each hurdle now comes from a distinct financial statement, so the MIN genuinely binds on different firms for different reasons, which is the condition under which a weakest-link aggregation can add information rather than noise.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Stock And Flow Anchor With Weakest Link
evaluated.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness should be measured against both what the firm owns and what it earns, because a stock anchor and a flow anchor misprice different firms; combining them gives a value leg on which the weakest-link quality screen can separate bargains from traps more reliably than either anchor alone.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the cosmetic industry-neutral swap with a substantive change to what is being priced, and it answers the earlier objection to multiple-averaging: book-to-market and EBITDA yield differ in numerator type — a balance-sheet stock versus an income flow — so their ranking errors are far less correlated than the earnings-versus-EBITDA pairing previously rejected. The archive also shows the two anchors have complementary strengths, with book-to-market producing the largest alphas when paired with balance-sheet conditioners and EBITDA yield the best Sharpe with the accounting conditioner, so the composite anchor is the natural way to capture both.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Four Hurdle Trap Score
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 0), ADD(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 0), ADD(INDICATOR(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(lt, at))), 0), INDICATOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale), 1)), 0))))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm's trap risk falls monotonically with the number of independent clean-bill tests it passes: honest depreciation recognition, cash covering near-term obligations, below-peer liability burden, and no build-up of non-cash working capital per dollar of sales.
evaluated.reasoning: Counting hurdles degrades gracefully as conditions are added, unlike MIN which binds on whichever leg is noisiest — this is why the two-hurdle count beat the weakest-link version on alpha — and all four conditions here are computable from balance-sheet and income-statement items, so coverage stays near 0.12 rather than collapsing as it did when the cash-flow-statement hurdle was added. The four tests draw on recognition policy, liquidity, solvency and the operating cycle, so they fail for genuinely different firms and the count is informative rather than a repeated measurement of one channel.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Enterprise Anchored Hurdle Count
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che)))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 0), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 0))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness of the operating business, measured against the whole capital structure rather than equity alone, is the anchor on which the quality hurdles should operate, because leveraged equity looks cheap for financing reasons that the hurdles are not designed to detect.
evaluated.reasoning: The stock-anchor test failed dramatically (book-to-market flipped the conjunctive alpha from +4.8% to -2.1%) while operating anchors succeeded, and enterprise value is the purest operating anchor available since it removes the mechanical leverage inflation that contaminates equity multiples. Its earlier pairing with an asset-composition conditioner produced 4.3% alpha, so testing it with the archive's strongest conditioner design determines whether the leading result can be improved by cleaning the value leg rather than the quality leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Peer Level Hurdle Substitution
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(dp, SUB(at, act))), 0), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 0))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The accounting hurdle should ask whether a cheap firm depreciates its long-lived assets faster than its industry peers, not whether it has recently changed its own practice, because chronically aggressive reporters never trip a self-benchmarked test yet are the most likely traps.
evaluated.reasoning: Self-benchmarking has a structural blind spot — a firm that has always used long useful lives shows no deviation — and the peer-benchmarked level was the one conditioner variant that produced independent positive alpha (2.6%, t=2.33) despite never being tested inside the winning count design. Substituting only the accounting hurdle while holding the liquidity hurdle and count aggregation fixed isolates which benchmark identifies traps better, which is the last unresolved measurement question in this family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sales Anchored Hurdle Count
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 0), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 0))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Revenue-based cheapness identifies firms the market has written off at the top line, including loss-makers that earnings-based multiples cannot rank, and the two clean-bill hurdles separate those with recoverable franchises from those in terminal decline.
evaluated.reasoning: Anchor choice has proven to be the single largest driver of sign in this archive — operating anchors work and the balance-sheet anchor inverts — so the final anchor question is whether the effect strengthens as the anchor moves further up the income statement, where accounting discretion has least influence on the multiple itself. Sales yield previously delivered 4.3% alpha with the continuous conditioner, and pairing it with the superior count design tests the anchor and the aggregation jointly at no cost to coverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Strict Hurdle Calibration Score
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)), 0.5), INDICATOR(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 1)), 0.5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm should only be credited with a clean bill of health when it clears each test by a visible margin rather than by a hair, so the hurdles should be set half a cross-sectional standard deviation above the break-even point rather than exactly at zero.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the double-weighted depreciation term the critic objected to and instead asks the one calibration question the count design leaves open — where the hurdles should sit — holding the two economic conditions, the aggregation and the value leg exactly fixed. Because a zero threshold classifies roughly half the cross-section as passing each test, tightening to a half-sigma margin concentrates the long leg on firms that are unambiguously clean, which should raise alpha if the trap mechanism is real and will attenuate it if the earlier result came from marginal firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unit Economics As Third Hurdle
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 0), ADD(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 0), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), MA(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 3)), 0)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm passes the third clean-bill test when its gross margin is holding at or above its own recent norm, showing that the discount reflects sentiment rather than eroding pricing power or rising input costs that no amount of accounting honesty or cash can offset.
evaluated.reasoning: The dividend flag was correctly identified as a size-age-profitability proxy rather than an independent test, so it is replaced by a firm-benchmarked margin condition that is measured entirely above the accrual line and is orthogonal to both the depreciation-policy hurdle and the liquidity hurdle. Benchmarking against the firm's own three-year margin rather than the cross-section removes the business-model differences that make gross margin levels a sector bet, so the hurdle fails for firms whose unit economics are actually deteriorating — the operating counterpart of the accounting trap.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Industry Neutral Sales Anchor Count
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 0), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 0))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Sales-to-price is mechanically determined by an industry's margin structure — a distributor and a software firm at identical mispricing have completely different sales yields — so ranking revenue cheapness within industry isolates genuine write-downs rather than sorting on where a firm sits in the value chain.
evaluated.reasoning: Industry neutralization was tested only on the EBITDA anchor, where margins differ far less across sectors and it cut alpha from 4.9% to 3.1%; for the sales anchor the confound it removes is first-order rather than second-order, so the same operator has a different expected effect and the test is not a repeat. The archive's sales-anchored count already achieves the best joint evidence, and its main weakness is a modest 0.28 Sharpe consistent with a persistent sector tilt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Enterprise Anchor With Floored Denominator
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MAX(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 0), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 0))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Enterprise cheapness is the right anchor for an operating-quality screen, but the enterprise value of a net-cash firm must not be allowed to collapse toward zero or turn negative, so it should be floored at market capitalization — a firm cannot be cheaper than its equity price implies simply because it holds cash.
evaluated.reasoning: The EV-anchored count produced the archive's largest alpha (6.2%, t=5.08) but the critic correctly identified that the denominator degenerates precisely for the cash-rich firms the liquidity hurdle rewards, so the extreme ranks may be an artifact rather than an economic signal. Flooring the denominator keeps the capital-structure neutrality that motivated the anchor while removing the degenerate region, which should preserve the alpha and clean up the cross-sectional slope.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sales Anchor With Margin Hurdle
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 0), ADD(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 0), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), MA(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 3)), 0)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: When cheapness is measured on revenue, the decisive additional question is whether that revenue still carries its usual margin: a firm cheap per dollar of sales with a gross margin at or above its own norm has recoverable earnings power, while one whose margin is eroding is cheap on revenue that will never convert to profit.
evaluated.reasoning: The margin hurdle diluted the EBITDA-anchored count because profitability is already embedded in that anchor, but it is exactly the missing information in a sales-based anchor, so this is a matched pairing rather than generic hurdle stacking. Its standalone third-hurdle version still produced 3.8% alpha with the archive's best count Sharpe (0.329), suggesting it adds portfolio stability where the sales anchor most needs it.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Peer Relative Hurdle Thresholds
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(IND_ZSCORE(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3))), 0), INDICATOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at)), 0))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The pass mark for each hurdle should be the industry norm rather than an absolute zero, because working-capital conventions make negative net cash normal in some industries and alarming in others, and depreciation revisions cluster within sectors when asset lives are reassessed industry-wide.
evaluated.reasoning: Absolute thresholds at zero mean the hurdles fire for whole sectors at once, which is likely behind the low Sharpe of the count family, whereas peer-relative thresholds make each firm compete against comparables and keep the count balanced within every industry. This tests threshold *definition* rather than threshold *strictness* — the latter was already tested and destroyed the slope (fmb -1.25) by shrinking the passing group, a failure mode industry demeaning does not share since it holds the pass rate near half by construction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Gross Profit Anchored Hurdle Count
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 0), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 0))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The right anchor for an accounting-quality screen is cheapness measured on the income line that management can least manipulate: gross profit sits above depreciation, overhead allocation and provisioning, so a low price per dollar of gross profit is a write-down of the underlying business rather than of a reported number.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the mechanical blend of two correlated anchors with a genuinely new anchor that sits economically between the two best performers — sales yield is too crude because it ignores whether revenue is profitable, EBITDA yield already absorbs overhead policy — and it is the anchor most complementary to a depreciation-discretion hurdle, since the two use non-overlapping parts of the income statement. Gross profit is also defined for firms with negative EBITDA, so the usable cross-section stays as wide as the sales-anchored version that currently produces the archive's best joint evidence.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Two Year Confirmed Hurdle Count
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(ADD(INDICATOR(MIN(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), LAG(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)), 0), INDICATOR(MIN(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), LAG(RATIO(SUB(che, lct), at), 1)), 0))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A hurdle is only informative if the firm clears it in consecutive years: a single year of above-norm depreciation or positive net cash can be an artifact of an asset sale or a financing round, whereas clearing the same test twice in a row identifies a durable policy and a durable funding position.
evaluated.reasoning: This keeps the discrete counting aggregation that has proven superior and the sales anchor that produces the strongest slope, and improves hurdle reliability through time-series confirmation rather than through a stricter cross-sectional cut — a distinction that matters because raising the threshold shrank the passing group and destroyed the slope (fmb -1.25), while requiring two consecutive passes removes transient classifications without unbalancing the groups. Reducing year-to-year churn in which firms pass should also lift the portfolio Sharpe, the one diagnostic on which the count family has been weakest.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Stability Scaled Cash Flow Yield
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 3)), RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(oancf, sale), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: The return to a high cash flow yield rises with the reliability of the cash flow stream; smoothed cash yield earned on a stable margin base is durable value, while an equally high but volatile yield is a one-off windfall the market correctly discounts.
considered.reasoning: Multiplying two bounded ranks makes the signal high only when persistent cheapness in cash terms coexists with low cash-margin volatility, a multiplicative rather than additive interaction. The three-year moving average removes transitory spikes in the valuation leg so the quality leg is measuring genuine process stability, not measurement noise.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheapness With Improving Profitability
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(TREND(RATIO(ib, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Cheap firms whose return on assets is on a rising five-year path are recovering franchises being mispriced, whereas equally cheap firms with a deteriorating profitability path are correctly priced declining businesses.
considered.reasoning: The trend operator supplies a dynamic quality state that a static profitability level cannot: it separates turnaround value from melting-ice-cube value within the same book-to-market decile. The product of ranks ensures the score is elevated only in the joint corner where both cheapness and improving fundamentals hold.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Depreciation Neutral Cash Backing Value
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(oancf, dp), ib), at), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: Earnings yield is rewarded only where reported income is persistently matched by depreciation-neutral cash earnings; when income runs ahead of cash earnings net of D&A, the low price reflects accrual-inflated, non-repeatable profits rather than mispricing.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the naive oancf > ib test with (oancf - dp) - ib removes the mechanical D&A addback that made the old gate switched on for nearly every firm, so the quality channel now splits the cross-section roughly evenly and genuinely discriminates. The gate is also made continuous and three-year smoothed, eliminating the degenerate zero mass point that previously sat in the middle of the sort, and the multiplicative rank form means cheapness only scores highly where cash backing is durable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Weakest Link Value Solvency
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), MIN(RANK(RATIO(re, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: A cheap stock is only a quality value stock if it also has accumulated retained earnings and enough operating cash flow to service its liabilities; a firm failing on any one leg is a distress candidate, so the score should be set by its weakest dimension rather than by an average.
considered.reasoning: The MIN operator is a conjunctive, weight-free aggregator that answers the arbitrary 50/25/25 weighting complaint directly: no strong leg can compensate for a weak one, which is exactly the value-trap logic that an additive composite dilutes. The quality legs are deliberately balance-sheet and debt-service based (retained earnings intensity, cash flow to total liabilities) rather than gross profitability and earnings stability, so this is not a repackaging of the published QMJ/Novy-Marx quality-value stack, and all inputs are contemporaneous so coverage stays high.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Quality Priced Only Among Cheap Firms
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, at)))
considered.hypothesis: Cash profitability is a much stronger return predictor inside the cheap segment than among richly valued firms, because low price plus strong cash generation is mispricing while low price plus weak cash generation is fundamental distress; expensive firms are informationally efficient on quality.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the earlier linear subtraction of two anomaly ranks with a true product of a non-negative cheapness rank and a signed industry quality z-score, so the long leg is cheap-and-cash-profitable, the short leg is cheap-and-cash-poor, and expensive firms collapse toward the neutral middle rather than populating a leg. The interaction is inseparable: the quality slope is scaled by the valuation rank, so neither leg alone reproduces the ordering, and industry normalization keeps the comparison among genuine peers.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap And Deteriorating Trap Score
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SUB(ZSCORE(WINSOR(GROWTH(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(ib, sale), 1), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, rising debt intensity combined with falling operating margin marks genuine deterioration and predicts underperformance, while cheap firms with deleveraging and improving margins are the recovering value names; the deterioration slope is steepest where valuation is lowest.
considered.reasoning: The old score was monotonically increasing in book-to-market because SUMRANK is non-negative; the deterioration term is now a signed, winsorized z-score difference that is centered at zero, so the sign of the product is set by fundamental deterioration and only its magnitude is amplified by cheapness. Expensive firms sit near zero regardless of their trajectory, so the short leg is cheap-and-deteriorating and the long leg is cheap-and-improving, making a negative slope both attainable and economically interpretable as the value-trap side of the value premium.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Conservative Earnings Yield
considered.expression: RATIO(MIN(ib, SUB(oancf, dp)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
considered.hypothesis: The market should be valued on the lower of reported income and depreciation-charged cash earnings; firms whose price is low relative to this conservative earnings base are cheap on the earnings number that is hardest to manage, whereas firms cheap only on reported income are accrual-inflated.
considered.reasoning: Subtracting dp before comparing to income neutralizes the D&A addback that made a naive oancf-versus-ib gate switch on almost everywhere, so the MIN genuinely binds for roughly half the cross-section and embeds the quality test inside the valuation multiple rather than beside it. Unlike the failed weakest-link rank screen, the MIN here operates on economic quantities in dollars, not on ranks, so it does not select stale low-growth firms and it produces a continuous, well-behaved yield variable that should sharpen the Fama-MacBeth slope.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap With Widening Gross Margin
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 5), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, a multi-year widening of the gross margin signals restored pricing power and mean-reverting mispricing, while a narrowing margin signals competitive erosion that justifies the low multiple.
considered.reasoning: The conditioner is a dynamic state (five-year slope of unit economics) rather than a level, which distinguishes recovering value from melting value in a way no static profitability or accrual measure can. Margin trend is measured before overhead and financing, so it is less contaminated by the earnings management that drives the accrual channels, making this an economically independent test.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Depreciation Conservatism Conditioned Earnings Yield
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, those charging depreciation at or above their own recent norm are reporting conservatively understated earnings and are genuinely cheap, while those whose depreciation intensity has fallen below their historical rate are propping up reported income through useful-life and write-off policy, so their low multiple is manufactured.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the gross-profitability conditioner that merely rediscovers Novy-Marx and QMJ and instead conditions value on an accounting-policy channel — the firm's own depreciation intensity relative to its three-year norm — which is a discretion-based quality measure rather than a profitability level. Benchmarking against the firm's own history rather than the cross-section removes capital-intensity differences, so the conditioner isolates policy change, and the signed z-score puts cheap-with-shrinking-depreciation firms in the short leg where the earnings-inflation trap lives.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Non Cash Working Capital Bloat Versus Sales
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale), 1), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A high EBITDA yield is a bargain only when each dollar of sales still requires the same or less non-cash working capital; when receivables and inventories net of operating payables rise per dollar of sales, the cheap firm is channel-stuffing or accumulating unsold goods and the discount is warranted.
considered.reasoning: The accrual measure is rebuilt as (act - che) - (lct - dlc), explicitly stripping cash and short-term debt so that cash accumulation or debt paydown is no longer misread as accrual bloat, fixing the internal inconsistency the critic identified. Expressing it as a change in working capital intensity of sales rather than a change scaled by assets makes it an operating-efficiency deterioration measure benchmarked to the firm's own revenue base, which is a sharper trap detector than the level accrual sort.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Earned Versus Contributed Book Value
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(re, ceq), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Book-to-market only identifies mispricing when the book value was earned rather than raised: a cheap firm whose equity is mostly accumulated retained earnings has demonstrated cash-generating capacity, while a cheap firm whose equity is mostly contributed capital has funded past losses with issuance and its book value carries no evidence of profitability.
considered.reasoning: The conditioner is the composition of book equity, not a leverage or solvency ratio, so it avoids the mechanical channel where debt inflates book-to-market and the sort degenerates into a leverage sort — the flaw in both the net-cash version and the earlier weakest-link screen. It also differs from the failed re/at screen because the scaling is by book equity, making it a capital-origin mix that is independent of asset size and of the value leg's own denominator.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Payer Only Dividend Sustainability Value
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(INDICATOR(dvc, 0), RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(oancf, dp), dvc), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Within dividend payers, a high yield is mispricing when operating cash flow net of the depreciation charge comfortably exceeds the dividend, and is a pre-cut trap when the payout consumes essentially all maintenance-adjusted cash generation.
considered.reasoning: The payer indicator forces non-payers to exactly zero, and since the conditioner is a signed z-score centered near zero the payers straddle them, so both portfolio legs are populated by dividend payers rather than by non-payers sorted on a solvency ratio. The coverage measure is now the payout tested against maintenance-adjusted cash earnings (oancf minus dp minus dvc) rather than against total liabilities, matching the sustainability mechanism in the hypothesis while using a safe assets denominator that avoids dividing by a zero dividend.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Depreciation Deviation With EBITDA Yield Leg
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, at), MA(RATIO(dp, at), 3)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The depreciation-conservatism conditioner should work with any pre-depreciation valuation multiple; pairing it with EBITDA yield tests whether the effect comes from the accounting-discretion channel rather than from the bottom-line earnings yield itself.
considered.reasoning: EBITDA yield is mechanically independent of the depreciation charge, so if the winning gen-1 signal were merely picking up the arithmetic link between dp and ib, this variant would fail, whereas if the discretion story is right it should be at least as strong and cleaner. This is a deliberate leg-isolation experiment that also avoids the negative-earnings tail that distorts E/P sorts.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Depreciation Lagging Asset Growth
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(GROWTH(dp, 1), GROWTH(at, 1)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, a depreciation charge growing more slowly than the asset base signals stretched useful lives and capitalized costs that flatter reported income, so the low multiple is on inflated earnings; depreciation growing with or ahead of assets marks conservative recognition and genuine cheapness.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the own-history level deviation of the gen-1 winner with a flow-versus-flow comparison, which detects under-depreciation of newly acquired assets that a level ratio can miss when the asset base is expanding. It keeps the discretion mechanism that worked while testing a different and more direct measurement of it, and uses only one-year changes so coverage stays close to the winner's 0.14.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Persistent Cash Earnings Within Cheap Book
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(SUB(oancf, dp), dvc), 0), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Book-to-market identifies mispricing among firms that have repeatedly generated cash earnings in excess of maintenance and payout needs, while cheap firms that have only intermittently self-funded are traps whose discount reflects a genuine funding gap.
considered.reasoning: This tests persistence — a count of self-funding years — rather than the level of accumulated equity that inverted in gen 1, distinguishing a repeated-outcome quality concept from a stock-of-safety concept. If persistence also inverts, we will have learned that any cheap-and-safe conditioner is spanned by FF5 and can retire the whole family; if it works, it opens a frequency-based dimension the archive has not used.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Gross Profit To Cash Conversion Value
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), SUB(sale, cogs)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What separates quality value from a value trap is how much of the gross profit actually survives overhead, working capital and maintenance capital to become distributable cash; a cheap firm converting a high fraction of gross profit into maintenance-adjusted cash flow is mispriced, one converting little is running an uneconomic cost structure.
considered.reasoning: Conversion efficiency is a ratio of two quality quantities rather than a scaled level, so it is orthogonal to the gross-profitability level that Novy-Marx documented and to the accrual measures already in the archive. Pairing it with EBITDA yield keeps the valuation leg independent of the depreciation and cash-flow terms in the conditioner, so the interaction is not mechanically induced.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Earnings Smoothing Versus Cash Volatility
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(VOL(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), at), 5), VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 5)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, those whose reported earnings are far smoother than their underlying maintenance-adjusted cash flows are using accrual discretion to mask a volatile business, so their low multiple rests on managed numbers; cheap firms whose earnings volatility matches their cash volatility are reporting honestly and are the genuine bargains.
considered.reasoning: This drops the operating-liability construct entirely, avoiding both the sign conflict with the accrual/NOA evidence and the overlap with the already-tested working-capital signal, and instead measures the gap between cash-flow variability and earnings variability — a second-moment discretion measure with no first-moment accrual content. It stays inside the accounting-discretion family that has produced the archive's only reliable alphas (depreciation deviation, cash backing) while testing smoothing rather than recognition timing, and the NEG makes the short leg cheap-and-heavily-smoothed firms.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Verifiable Asset Backing Of Cheap Book
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(act, at), 1)))
